node.label: Patrick Joyce
node.date_label: Work, Society and Politics 1980 · Visions of the People 1991 · “History and Post-Modernism” 1991 · Democratic Subjects 1994 · Class (Oxford Reader) 1995 · “The End of Social History?” 1995 · The Social in Question (ed.) 2002 · The Rule of Freedom 2003 · “What Is the Social in Social History?” 2010 · The State of Freedom 2013 · Going to My Father's House 2021 · Remembering Peasants 2024
node.description: A British social historian whose Visions of the People (1991) held that 'the fixation with class' had denied historians 'sight of these other visions of the social order'. Against the 'received wisdom' fixed by Thompson and Hobsbawm, he found in industrial England a 'family of populisms' whose 'controlling narrative' concerned 'a righteous and dispossessed "people" rather than a "working class"'; popular Liberalism and Toryism were 'about the union of the classes against class'. Democratic Subjects (1994) deepened his 'engagement with "post-modernist" theory'. 'The End of Social History?' (1995) put identity, modernity and structure to the field as 'areas where the challenge of post-modernist thought was especially evident'; Eley and Nield answered, and he denied any purpose to 'bury' Marxism and class. Tilly called him a 'softcore' solipsist still captive to Thompson; Cannadine, as Joyce reported, wanted 'a history of status'. The Rule of Freedom (2003) and The State of Freedom (2013) turned to Foucauldian governmentality and a 'new materialism' (Koditschek: 'with an assist from Bruno Latour'); in 2010 he recalled a debate in which 'heat exceeded light'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Patrick Joyce (b. 1945); Work, Society and Politics (1980); Visions of the People: Industrial England and the Question of Class, 1848–1914 (1991); 'History and Post-Modernism' (Past and Present 133, 1991); 'The Imaginary Discontents of Social History' (Social History, 1993); Democratic Subjects (1994); ed., Class (Oxford Readers, 1995); 'The End of Social History?' (Social History 20, 1995) and 'A Brief Reply to Eley and Nield' (1996); 'More Secondary Modern than Postmodern' (Rethinking History, 2001); ed., The Social in Question (2002); The Rule of Freedom (2003); 'What Is the Social in Social History?' (Past and Present 206, 2010); The State of Freedom (2013); 'History and Governmentality' (Análise Social, 2014); Going to My Father's House (2021); Remembering Peasants (2024). Readers: David Cannadine (1992–93); Charles Tilly (1994); Neville Kirk (1994); Geoff Eley and Keith Nield (1995; 2000; 2007); Theodore Koditschek (2014); Andrew Miles, Dave O'Brien and Mike Savage (2014); James Vernon (2016).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-22 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-joyce-vernon-lawrence.md, Part A): Visions of the People in its Cambridge description and contents and the openings of the introduction and chapters 3, 4 and 14 (through the chapter DOIs), with further passages (pp. 4, 8, 11, 14, 96, 331–332) as quoted by Tilly (1994, read in full); Democratic Subjects, Class, The Social in Question, The Rule of Freedom and The State of Freedom in publisher descriptions and contents only; the 1996 reply, the 2010 Past & Present article and the 2010 BJS piece in their opening paragraphs; 'History and Governmentality' (2014) in full; the 1993 NYRB letter and Cannadine's reply in full; the 2011 foreword in full; the 2001 ego-histoire in its abstract; Koditschek (2014) in full; Eley and Nield (2000) in full (spread research). Unread: 'The End of Social History?' (1995), Eley and Nield's 'Starting Over' (1995), Kirk (1994), Steinberg (1996), the 1993 note, the 1991 Past & Present piece, the Miles–O'Brien–Savage symposium (2014), Vernon's 2016 essay beyond its first sentence, and the bodies of every book; Taylor & Francis and Oxford pages were inaccessible. The 1995 article's content is given only as Joyce himself summarised it in 1996; his denial that he meant to bury class is recorded with the critiques. Born 1945 in Paddington (Wikidata); Balliol College, Oxford; the Manchester affiliation from his 1991 and 1993 signatures and the 2008 retirement conference. Not to be confused with P. W. Joyce (1827–1914), the Irish historian.

proposed_edges.relationship: 'The End of Social History?' (1995) put identity, modernity and structure to social history as 'areas where the challenge of post-modernist thought was especially evident'; he denied any purpose 'to "dismiss" or "bury" Marxism, class and social history' (1996) and in 2010 recalled a debate in which 'heat exceeded light'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: the 1996 reply, p. 96 (opening read): 'It is good that Eley and Nield's response to my article on the future of social history opens up a space for debate between post-modernist and earlier positions'; 'It is not my purpose to "dismiss" or "bury" Marxism, class and social history, as should be plain from the article'; the points of substance 'phrased in terms of identity, modernity and structure'. 2010, p. 213 (opening read): 'Much of the 1990s' debate was vigorous and productive. Some of it, though, was vigorous and unproductive … Heat exceeded light'. The 1995 article is unread; its questions are known only from his 1996 summary. Eley and Nield's 'Starting Over' (1995) is unread; their 2000 essay (read) welcomes 'the critique of social explanation and the necessity of all the debates mobilized by Joyce and Stedman Jones' (p. 16).

proposed_edges.relationship: Visions of the People (1991) against the chronology of class fixed by Thompson and Hobsbawm: 'the fixation with class' denied sight of 'other visions of the social order'; 'because manual workers chose to wear cloth caps and support football teams, it does not follow that they saw the social order in terms of class' (p. 8, as quoted by Tilly)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: introduction p. 1 (chapter opening read): 'while there is no denying that class was a child of the nineteenth century, when it comes to how the social order was represented and understood, there were other children too who were every bit as lusty as class'; p. 8 as quoted by Tilly (1994, p. 264, read in full), against Hobsbawm; ch. 14 opening (p. 329): 'rather than a single populism, it is a variety or "family" of populisms that should be considered'; 'The controlling narrative of popular politics appears to have concerned a righteous and dispossessed "people" rather than a "working class"'. Tilly's judgement that 'by most standards he has also documented the salience of working-class identities' (p. 265) is the counterweight. The book's body is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson's Making 'presents a picture of class consciousness as substantially "made" by around 1830'; this 'received wisdom has in fact become a dead weight' (1991). Tilly answered that Joyce and Vernon 'remain captives of Thompson' and 'engage in Thompsonian hermeneutics' (1994)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, introduction p. 1 (chapter opening read): 'the work of E. P. Thompson and E. J. Hobsbawm remained, and remains, central, fixing the historical sequence of class development … Received wisdom has in fact become a dead weight, the fixation with class denying us sight of these other visions of the social order.' Tilly 1994, pp. 262–263 (read in full): 'Joyce and Vernon nevertheless remain captives of Thompson … They engage in Thompsonian hermeneutics'; 'it was Thompson above all who argued that class was not an individual state of mind … but a dynamic, contested relationship among sets of people'. Hobsbawm is named in the same sentence; no separate arrow is drawn to him.

proposed_edges.relationship: Class read as narrative and discourse: a 'master narrative' of 'an excluded and virtuous people' (1991, pp. 331–332, as quoted by Tilly); Democratic Subjects (1994) 'a deepening of … engagement with "post-modernist" theory'; the 1995 reader Class placed Stedman Jones, Scott and Sewell beside Baudrillard's 'The End of the Social'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Visions pp. 331–332 as quoted by Tilly (1994, pp. 264–265, read): 'it is better to talk of a "master narrative" rather than of a "master identity"'; 'an excluded and virtuous people doing battle in its pilgrim's progress against the forces of privilege, faction, darkness and ignorance'. Cambridge description of Democratic Subjects (read): 'a deepening of Patrick Joyce's engagement with "post-modernist" theory'. Class (1995): contents via Crossref; 'Narratives of Class' opening, p. 322 (read): 'Class identities were, therefore, a product of arguments about meanings, arguments which were primarily political in character'. Eley and Nield (2000, p. 6, read) read Democratic Subjects as 'a redeployed intellectual history based on restricted readings of the printed word'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Popular Liberalism and Toryism 'were about the union of the classes against class' (1991); 'The Constitution and the Narrative Structure of Victorian Politics' in Vernon's Re-reading the Constitution (1996); The State of Freedom (2013) as 'a pioneering new approach to political history in which social and material factors are centre stage'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ch. 3 opening of Visions (read): Gladstone's 'crusade of the "masses" against the "classes"'; 'Popular Liberalism, and in fact popular Toryism as well, were about the union of the classes against class.' Re-reading the Constitution: contents read (ch. 7 is Joyce's). Cambridge description of The State of Freedom (read): 'both a pioneering new approach to political history in which social and material factors are centre stage, and a highly original history of modern Britain'. Bodies unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Governmentality: Foucault's 'Governmentality', Gordon, Burchell and Rose anthologised in his Class (1995); The Rule of Freedom 'develops Foucauldian approaches to historiography' (2003); governmentality as 'a kind of intellectual machinery or apparatus for rendering reality thinkable', though prone to 'crypto-functionalism' (2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: 'History and Governmentality' (2014, read in full), quoting Rose: governmentality 'concerns the ways in which those who would exercise rule have posed to themselves the question' of how to govern; 'a kind of intellectual machinery or apparatus for rendering reality thinkable'; governmentality studies 'suffered also from a tendency to a sort of crypto-functionalism'; 'In developing the work of Foucault alongside the new materialism, I and my recent collaborator Chandra Mukerji begin from the assertion' that modern states are impersonal social formations. BJS 2010 (opening read) reprises Rose and Miller. Verso description of The Rule of Freedom (read): 'creatively and originally develops Foucauldian approaches to historiography'. Class (1995) contents: Foucault's 'Governmentality' (pp. 201–203), Gordon and Burchell, Donzelot, Rose. Koditschek (2014, read): The State of Freedom 'draws largely on the ideas of Michel Foucault'.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Social in Question (2002) printed Latour's case for replacing 'the social' with 'association'; Joyce later named 'science studies' and 'the new materialism' as what he took up 'alongside' Foucault (2014); Koditschek read The State of Freedom as Foucault 'with an assist from Bruno Latour' (2014)
proposed_edges.map_label: Science studies and the new materialism, 2002–14
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Moderate. Latour's chapter in Joyce's 2002 volume (read for 1.151, w3_latour_tarde_2002): ANT as 'a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word "social" in social theory to replace it with the word "association"'; Joyce's printing it is an editorial choice, and his introduction is unread. His own 2014 words (read in full) name 'science studies' and 'the various elements that make up what is being called the new materialism', with Timothy Mitchell as the example, not Latour. Koditschek (JBS 2014, read) names Latour: the book 'draws largely on the ideas of Michel Foucault (with an assist from Bruno Latour)'. The 2011 foreword (read): 'a new awakening of interest in the nature of materiality in relation to power'.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Rule of Freedom (2003): the liberal governance of the nineteenth-century city 'depended on the "rule of freedom"', read through 'maps and censuses, sewers and markets, public libraries and parks' in London and Manchester
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Verso description (read 2026-10-22): 'The liberal governance of the nineteenth-century state and city depended on the "rule of freedom"'; the city's 'layout, architecture, infrastructure' and 'such artifacts as maps and censuses, sewers and markets, public libraries and parks' examined for 'the impersonal, often invisible forms of social direction and control built into the infrastructure of modern life'. The body is unread; Cohen (AHR 2004) and Frohman (CJH 2004) are metadata only. Moderate: a publisher's statement of the book's argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: From the linguistic turn to material culture: the city's infrastructure as 'impersonal, often invisible forms of social direction' (2003); 'cultural history' as 'an important historiographical force' after the 1990s, with 'the partial eclipse of "social history"' (2010); 'a new awakening of interest in the nature of materiality in relation to power' (2011)
proposed_edges.map_label: Material culture after the cultural turn, 2003–11
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: 2010, p. 213 (opening read): 'One in particular has been the emergence of "cultural history" as an important historiographical force, while another has been the partial eclipse of "social history"'; 2011 foreword, p. xi (read in full): 'The intellectual agenda that follows embraces postcolonial and post-Foucault governmentality perspectives, for instance, and a new awakening of interest in the nature of materiality in relation to power'. Verso 2003 description (read). Koditschek (2014, read) calls The State of Freedom 'a masterpiece of theoretically informed historical analysis' while finding its approach 'class-evacuated'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Vernon credited Joyce as an adviser and continuing intellectual influence: 'As an adviser he was a constant catalyst for thought and conversation, and his scholarship continues to inform our work' (Gunn and Vernon, 2011, on the conference held 'to honor Patrick Joyce on the occasion of his retirement'); Vernon's 2016 essay took Joyce's 'secondary modern' title
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gunn and Vernon 2011, acknowledgments p. ix (read in full; co-signed with Gunn; it establishes advisory influence, not doctoral supervision): the conference 'Liberal Subjects: The Politics of Social and Cultural History since the 1970s' (Manchester, March 2008) 'to honor Patrick Joyce on the occasion of his retirement'; 'As an adviser he was a constant catalyst for thought and conversation'. Vernon 2016 (title and opening sentence): 'As Patrick Joyce is a scholar who likes to say a lot with the titles of his work I take my own from his ego-histoire'. The influence coexists with disagreement: Politics and the People found identities 'not done justice by Patrick Joyce's "family of populisms"' (p. 297, as quoted by Tilly 1994).

proposed_edges.relationship: Joyce's 'pioneering early work on the rise of a new urban paternalism in the factory politics of Lancashire' (Work, Society and Politics, 1980) used as evidence that 'corporate' identities persisted in Britain's 'conservative modernity' (2011)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lawrence 2011, p. 150 (read in full): cites 'Patrick Joyce's pioneering early work on the rise of a new urban paternalism in the factory politics of Lancashire' as evidence for the persistence of corporate identities under 'Tory liberalism'. A use of the 1980 book as evidence, not an acknowledged debt; the book itself is unread. Moderate.
